Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Fawn Response: become overly compliant when feeling threatened
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Keisha was nineteen when the storm broke. It had started as a routine Saturday evening, the air thick and heavy, until the sky collapsed. Rain lashed against the windows in sheets so dense she could not see the streetlights. The power died without warning, plunging her bedroom into absolute dark. Water rose faster than the sump pump could push it out. She clung to the top stair, the wind screaming like a living thing, the sound of shattering glass and collapsing roof tiles echoing in her chest. When the water finally receded, leaving debris and silence in its wake, the storm had taken her neighborhood, but the night itself had stayed with her. She came to believe that darkness was no longer safe, that the sky could open without warning, and that ordinary weather carried the same silent threat she had felt kneeling on that wet staircase. Over the months that followed, Keisha’s world narrowed. She began avoiding the gym, trading her usual post-class runs for long walks along familiar, sheltered streets. When she tried to push through, her body rebelled: her pulse would spike, her breath would shorten, and a familiar tightness would coil in her stomach the moment the wind picked up. She stopped speaking about the flood. She had come to believe that showing fear would only invite more collapse, so she learned to clamp down on every flicker of expression. When colleagues asked if she was alright, she offered a steady nod, her voice flat, her shoulders rigid. She told herself it was discipline. It felt like survival. Now, at twenty-one, Keisha worked in the surgical wing of a metropolitan hospital. The environment demanded precision, but her attention had fractured into a thousand quiet scans. She noticed the emergency generator kick in every time a summer squall rolled past the high windows. When the overhead lights flickered, her breath caught instantly. A dropped chart, a sudden pager vibration, the sharp crack of a door closing down the hall—each sent her shoulders hiking toward her ears, her body bracing before her mind could register the harmless source. She could not stop herself from watching the exits, counting staff movements, tracking the rhythm of every alarm. She was certain that if she looked away for even a moment, something irreversible would happen. In the operating room, where certainty was supposed to be absolute, Keisha found herself yielding easily. When the attending’s voice rose during a scrub-in, she felt the familiar spike of threat. Her response was to smooth her posture, nod too quickly, and echo every directive without hesitation, even when her hands already knew the next step. She could not trust her own instincts anymore. She had come to believe she could not rely on herself, that her judgment was fractured beyond repair. She stopped raising concerns in team huddles. She avoided mentoring junior residents. Her life, she thought, had been unspooled by the flood. She couldn’t stop bad things from happening, and trying to hold it all together only made her hands shake. What finally brought Keisha to my office was a Tuesday evening power outage in the hospital. The backups hummed to life, but in that half-minute of blackout, she had dropped a scalpel, her heart hammering against her ribs, her vision tunneling. She stood in the dark corridor, waiting for a ceiling to cave in, for water to rise, for the storm to return. When the lights flickered back on, she walked out of her shift, called in sick for the next three days, and booked an appointment. She told herself she was seeking clarity, but what she most hoped for was a way to stop bracing for the next collapse. She most feared that she would never again feel safe in the dark, in the storm, or inside her own body.
